title: Trump-Xi AI Summit Looms as OpenAI, Nvidia and Qualcomm CEOs Head to Washington, While Huawei's New York Trial Opens
subhead: The September 24 White House summit puts AI governance and chip export policy at the center of the world's defining rivalry, even as the US government's long-running criminal case against Huawei finally goes to trial in New York.

sections.heading: The Trump-Xi Summit Turns Into a Tech Negotiating Table
sections.body:
With the September 24 White House summit days away, artificial intelligence and advanced chips have moved to the top of the US-China agenda. Per POLITICO (cited by News18 and the Foreign Policy Journal), OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon are expected to attend Trump's state dinner with Xi Jinping, an unusually direct signal that technology leaders will sit in the room during the negotiations. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed Altman's attendance; Qualcomm confirmed Amon's.

The stakes are concrete. Reuters reports Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to raise AI and rare earths with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng as the tech rivalry widens. For Huang, the unspoken backdrop is access to the Chinese market for Nvidia's advanced processors — he has personally lobbied the White House and Congress to allow sales of its most capable chips to China. Altman and Huang also sit on opposite sides of the AI-safety debate heading into the meeting, with Altman backing Anthropic's Dario Amodei's calls for an industrywide slowdown and Huang dismissing catastrophic-risk warnings as 'hysterical.'
sections.whyItMatters: A summit framed around AI and chip exports is a qualitative shift: the two biggest economies are now negotiating the rules of the compute race directly, with the CEOs who control the hardware and models in the room. Whatever emerges — or fails to — will set the tone for export controls and model-safety standards for the rest of the year.

sections.heading: Huawei's Criminal Trial Finally Opens in New York
sections.body:
Nearly eight years after the Department of Justice unsealed its indictment, Huawei's criminal trial is underway in the Eastern District of New York, and prosecutors are pulling no punches. According to the ICIJ's China Capital investigation, DOJ prosecutor Taylor Stout has labeled Huawei a 'criminal enterprise' running 'a far-reaching criminal scheme extending over twenty years' — arguing 'crime was an important business strategy.' The company faces 12 felony charges, including conspiring to steal technology from US rivals and lying to Western banks about business in Iran in violation of sanctions.

The trial has already surfaced stark testimony. Parham Baheshti, a former engineer at Iranian telecom firm Mobinet, testified that Huawei, working with Iranian intelligence, built a domestic surveillance system able to spy on wireless users — telling jurors the company helps 'a dictatorship to rule and suppress people.' Huawei's defense (led by Brian Heberlig, one of at least a dozen attorneys) counters that the case concerns 'disconnected incidents' and is 'about competition, not conspiracy.' ICIJ notes the DOJ plans to introduce former CFO Meng Wanzhou's 2021 deferred-prosecution admission that she lied to HSBC about Huawei's Iran business. Judge Ann Donnelly told jurors 'China and the Chinese Communist Party are not on trial,' but expects the case to run through Christmas or into next year.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first time the US has put Huawei in an actual courtroom rather than settling or relying on export controls and blacklists. A conviction on trade-secret theft would arm Washington with a legal precedent for the broader 'technology theft' allegations behind its AI sanctions push — a case being watched closely in Beijing.

sections.heading: SpaceX Prepares Starship's First Orbital Flight — With Starlink Payload
sections.body:
SpaceX has pushed Starship's 14th test flight, its first orbital mission, to around September 28 (originally slated for the 22nd), pending regulatory approval, per mynews13 and New Scientist. The flight will send the 407-foot stack from Boca Chica, Texas, on a near-10-hour mission circling Earth about six times at roughly 171 miles altitude — a first that shifts Starship from suborbital test vehicle to a candidate for fully rapid reuse.

The mission also carries a commercial payload: 26 Starlink V3 satellites, each adding 1 terabit per second of capacity for a combined 26 Tbps added in a single launch. Three of the satellites carry cameras to scan Starship's heatshield during re-entry, and two recovered tiles from the previous flight are being reflown for the first time. The flight follows Ship 13's drawn-out Indian Ocean water landing, which gave SpaceX data on heatshield improvements.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first Orbital-class demonstration of the launch vehicle SpaceX plans to use for Artemis III and high-volume Starlink deployment. Reaching orbit with working V3 satellites aboard tests whether Starship can become the workhorse that densifies Starlink capacity — and whether its launch economics remain unmatched for the foreseeable future.

sections.heading: Foreign Hackers Breached Two Colorado Water Utilities
sections.body:
Colorado Governor Jared Polis's office confirmed on Friday that foreign hackers targeted and manipulated equipment in two local water systems last month, according to Reuters (via MSN and Fox News). The breachers altered pumping cycles and disabled alarms before operators regained control. The governor's office stressed that, to the state's knowledge, 'treatment processes and water quality were not impacted at either provider.'

The incident adds to a pattern of attacks on US water infrastructure, and the Denver Post notes the state is weighing Iran-related concerns given the broader regional escalation. It comes against a backdrop of repeated federal warnings that US utilities remain soft targets for state-sponsored actors, with the Council on Foreign Relations publishing fresh guidance on how to harden American critical infrastructure against Chinese cyber threats.
sections.whyItMatters: The attack targeted operational technology — pumping and alarm systems — not just data, which is the threshold that separates espionage from genuine infrastructure disruption. That Colorado officials flagged the possibility of foreign-state involvement shows how cyberattacks on basic utilities are being read through the lens of great-power rivalry.

sections.heading: Chip Industry Faces a 157,000-Worker Shortfall as Intel Pitches US Customers
sections.body:
The US semiconductor industry is staring at a 157,000-worker shortfall by 2030, according to McKinsey and the SEMI Foundation, with only about 3% of US engineering graduates entering chipmaking even as dozens of new fabs come online this decade (via MSN and Startup Fortune). Samsung and Micron are reportedly paying large retention bonuses to hold onto scarce talent.

On the technology front, Piper Sandler reports Intel's 14A process is being evaluated by Amazon, Apple, AMD, Google, Tesla, Microsoft, Nvidia and Qualcomm (per Wccftech), positioning Intel as a US onshore alternative at a moment TSMC's advanced capacity is 'choked' until at least 2028. Separately, Samsung has moved about 10% of Galaxy Z Fold 8 component production to October amid a chip shortage, per SammyFans.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is building fabs faster than it can staff them — a bottleneck that undercuts the CHIPS-driven onshoring strategy. Meanwhile Intel's push to get its most advanced process validated by the biggest US customers is the strongest sign yet that the AI-chip foundry race is now a genuine three-way fight between TSMC, Samsung and Intel.

sections.heading: Critical Minerals: US Investment Fails to Dent China's Grip
sections.body:
Despite fresh US government initiatives, China still dominates the supply chain for critical minerals essential to clean energy, according to a Reuters analysis published this week at the RE-EII event. Washington's investment push is not yet translating into meaningful supply security. The Democratic Republic of Congo, which holds some of the world's richest reserves, continues to be held back by power, rail and processing bottlenecks (via MSN and Jason Mitchell's reporting), capturing less than 1% of clean-energy value despite holding roughly 30% of global critical-mineral reserves.

Separately, the run-up to Xi's Washington visit has put BYD, CATL and Xiaomi in the mix for a possible trip alongside the Chinese leader, per MSN/Reuters, as Canada and the US diverge over access for Chinese EVs — a reminder that critical minerals and EV market access travel together in the trade talks.
sections.whyItMatters: The bottleneck is processing, not mining — and China owns the processing. US spending alone won't break that dependency, which is why the mineral question is increasingly part of the AI and technology agenda between Washington and Beijing rather than a stand-alone energy issue.

bottomLine: The defining development today is that the US-China rivalry is moving to the negotiating table: the September 24 Trump-Xi summit has AI and chip access at its core, and OpenAI, Nvidia and Qualcomm CEOs are expected in the room. That diplomatic track is running parallel to the legal track, with Huawei finally on trial in New York for alleged trade-secret theft and Iran sanctions violations. Add Starship's first orbital flight set for the 28th, a fresh breach of two Colorado water utilities, and a US chip industry facing a 157,000-worker staffing gap, and the picture is a technology race being fought simultaneously in courtrooms, orbital pads, water plants and Washington state dinners.
sources: POLITICO via News18, Foreign Policy Journal, Crypto Briefing, Reuters (Bessent/Colorado water/critical minerals), ICIJ China Capital, mynews13, New Scientist, MSN (chip workforce), Wccftech, SammyFans, Fox News, Denver Post, Council on Foreign Relations, MSN/Reuters (EVs)
